Where things stand

Seychelles' best Indian restaurant, on a website phones can't read

Lonely Planet picks The Maharajas as the best Indian restaurant in Seychelles. Most people who look you up, visitors especially, do it on a phone, and today's site was built before phones mattered.

What a phone shows today

  • The site isn't built for phones. Phones get the full computer page shrunk to fit the screen, so the writing is a few millimetres tall and people have to pinch and zoom to read anything.
  • The menu is 14 pictures. Every dish and price sits inside an image. It's hard to read on a phone, and Google can't read it at all, so someone searching for "butter chicken Eden Island" won't find your menu.
  • Takeaway is offered, but there's no way to order. The home page says take away facilities are available. The only way to order is to call.

Small things that add up

  • The opening hours disagree. The same page says "Open 7 days a week" and "Tuesday to Sunday: 12 noon to 10 pm".
  • The same paragraph appears four times on the home page, and the Twitter box beside it is empty.
  • The code underneath dates from around 2011. It still carries a warning bar for Internet Explorer 6.
  • Your Facebook page has beautiful recent food photos. None of them are on the website.
Why a website matters for The Maharajas

What a great site does for a restaurant

People decide where to eat on their phones, often the same afternoon, from a hotel room or a boat in the marina. A website is where that decision can end with a table booked at The Maharajas.

Found first

Where visitors choose dinner

"Indian restaurant Seychelles", "Eden Island restaurants", "biryani near me". A menu written as real text gives Google something to show, with your hours, location and phone number beside it.

Know what to expect

People book what they can picture

North Indian food is new to many visitors. Real photos beside each course show what a malai tikka or a biryani looks like, so ordering feels easy before they've even arrived.

Takeaway

Orders in writing, not over the phone

Eden Island residents choose their dishes, see the total and send the order on WhatsApp with a collection time. Fewer misheard orders during the dinner rush.

Bookings

A table in a few taps

Name, date, time and guests, plus "a table by the marina, if one is free", sent to you at any hour. Nobody has to wait for opening time to call.

First impressions

A site that matches the dining room

The Maharajas is a special night out. When the website feels the same, guests arrive expecting something special, and the price makes sense before they sit down.

The view

Sell the table by the marina

Yachts, the Mahé mountains and the sunset are part of the meal. The site shows that table at dusk, so visitors can picture the evening.

Groups

Birthdays and company dinners

Private and corporate dinners get their own place on the site, with a button to ask about a date, so bigger bookings find you too.

Works with social

Somewhere to send everyone

Your Instagram bio, Facebook posts, WhatsApp chats and Google Maps can all lead to one place with the whole menu, the photos and a way to book.

The new site

Scroll and the table is served

A North Indian meal comes in courses, so the site does too. As you scroll, a brass thali on a table above the marina fills itself course by course: soups and street food, the tandoor, curries, rice and biryani, breads, then desserts and mango lassi. The evening moves on as you go, from the sunset behind the Mahé mountains to the lights of Victoria. Saffron points on each dish open that course's full menu.

The full site is live for you to try. Open it on your phone, scroll through the courses, open a menu page and put a takeaway order together. It's on a private preview address and isn't listed on Google.
https://socialmedia-seychelles.github.io/reviews/maharajas-concept/

Open the live site

Every course arrives on screen

A brass ladle pours the soup and each curry. Samosas and papad land on the plate, the sizzler slides in with a burst of smoke, basmati rains onto the thali, naans flip down, butter melts and gulab jamuns roll into their syrup. A jug pours the mango lassi.

Most restaurant websites are a page of text and a phone number. This one is something people show each other at the table.

Real photos of your dishes

Each course page opens with photos from your own Facebook page, so visitors can see what to expect before they order. The first sits in a pointed arch with a fine brass line, and the rest slide sideways.

We'd only put them live with your OK. A food shoot can add more: the soups page doesn't have a photo yet.

Tap a photo to see it up close

Any photo opens full screen with the dish name. Visitors swipe through the rest of the course, and each photo links back to your post on Facebook, which sends people to your page as well.

Your whole menu, as text

All 89 dishes and prices from your 14 menu pictures are typed up, with the descriptions and vegetarian and non-vegetarian marks. They're easy to read on any phone, and Google can find them.

Every dish has an Add button for takeaway.

Takeaway orders on WhatsApp

One order follows visitors across the site, from course to course. They see the total, choose a collection time, add a note ("medium spicy, please") and send it to your WhatsApp or by email.

There's no online payment and nothing new for the team to learn: you confirm the time and they pay when they collect, just as they do now.

Book a table, find the way

The booking form asks for the date, time and number of guests, offers a table by the marina if one is free, and asks if they're celebrating. It arrives on WhatsApp or by email.

The last step has your hours, phone numbers, a map, the Lonely Planet line and private and corporate dinners.

On phones, the course text sits in a card under the table, with the Menu and My order buttons always at the top. Phones that can't show the 3D table still get every course, the menu and ordering, on a plain background.

Questions

Things you might be wondering

Do we keep our web address and email?

Yes. The new site goes live on themaharajasseychelles.com. We'll set it up with your current host so your email addresses keep working as they are.

How do we change prices or dishes?

Send us the changes on WhatsApp or by email and we'll update the site. We'll talk through an aftercare option on the call, so updates are always quick.

Do we have to manage online payments?

No. Orders and bookings arrive on WhatsApp or by email, your team confirms them, and guests pay at the restaurant as they do now. Online payments can be added later if you ever want them.

Where do the photos come from?

From your public Facebook page. Each course page credits it and every photo links to its post. We'd only put them live with your OK, and a food shoot can replace them or add more.

Is the food on the thali a photo?

No. The thali and its dishes are drawn in 3D, so they can be served and animated as you scroll. The real photos of your food are on each course page.

What if we want something different from the concept?

Tell us on the call. Small changes are free once you buy the site, and anything bigger is quoted before we start, so there are no surprises.

Will it work on older phones?

Yes. Phones that can't show the 3D table still get every course, the full menu, ordering and booking.
